clue.text: Amino acid tipped for synthesis in volcanic island

indicators.note: synthesis puts the letters together into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: tipped means the tip, its opening letter, is knocked off

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A chemist's note about an amino acid being supplied for a synthesis on a volcanic isle.
explanation.walkthrough: ACID loses its tip A to leave CID; with AMINO those letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Dominica is a mountainous Caribbean island of volcanic origin.

clue.text: Playing autoharp; regrettably a pro's left it in a state

indicators.note: playing the autoharp suggests its letters are moved about
regrettably shows the letters of a pro are jumbled too, before they come out
left means these letters have gone from the instrument

explanation.surface: A professional plays the autoharp badly and walks off in a temper.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove A, P, R and O, in any order, from AUTOHARP, and the remaining letters rearrange to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Utah is one of the fifty United States.

clue.text: Using cunning, zip about No 4 in Second Eleven

indicators.note: Something placed about another thing is wrapped round it, so these letters open up and take the rest inside.

parts.note: to zip about is to fly about

indicators.note: Asking for No 4 in a word asks for its fourth letter and nothing else.

parts.note: the fourth letter of SECOND
XI is eleven in Roman numerals, and the way a cricket or football side of eleven is written

explanation.surface: An instruction to a reserve team's number four: be sly, and keep moving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second Eleven' looks like one cricketing unit and is two separate jobs — one word gives up a single letter, the other its Roman numerals. A second eleven is a club's reserve side.
explanation.definitionFit: To act foxily is to act with a fox's cunning, the adverb standing in for 'slyly'.

clue.text: Dance, as Marillion song on the radio

indicators.note: Something on the radio reaches you as sound only, so it is the way the word is said that matters, not the way it is spelt.

parts.note: Marillion's 1985 hit was 'Kayleigh', and the Gaelic dance is said in exactly that way

explanation.surface: Dancing away to a Marillion track coming out of the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: Marillion are the British rock band whose 'Kayleigh' reached number two in 1985, and that girl's name is the dance's spelling turned phonetic. A ceilidh is an evening of Scottish or Irish dancing with a caller.
explanation.definitionFit: A ceilidh is a social evening of Scottish and Irish dancing, so the bare word 'dance' names the event.

clue.text: A drowned valley that's conveyed by piping

definitions.note: The answer is a thing and the definition a description of it rather than a synonym: an aria is something carried on a high clear voice, which is what piping means here.

parts.note: the clue's opening word taken as the letter it is
the geographer's word for a river valley flooded by the sea, as at Falmouth or Milford Haven

explanation.surface: A flooded valley whose water arrives through a pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piping' is plumbing on the surface and a voice in the answer — to pipe is to sing high and clear. The geography is real: a ria is a drowned river valley.
explanation.definitionFit: An aria is a solo song in an opera, delivered on a singer's pipes rather than spoken.

clue.text: Deduce spoof largely concocted with AI instructions?

indicators.note: concocted means made up, so these letters are mixed together
largely means most of the word is used, its last letter dropped

explanation.surface: Working out that a hoax was mostly cooked up by artificial intelligence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'largely' cuts SPOOF to SPOO, and 'concocted' rearranges DEDUCE plus SPOO.
explanation.definitionFit: Pseudocode is program logic written informally, the kind of step-by-step instructions one might give an AI model.

clue.text: Hopefully, with finale from tenor to replace bass, producing calm

indicators.note: A finale is the last thing to happen, so what is wanted from the word is its closing letter.
One thing replacing another takes over its place exactly, so the new letter sits where the old one sat.

parts.note: 'at best' is how you put the most hopeful reading of a situation
B is the music shorthand for bass, and it is the letter that has to go
the finale of TENOR, its closing letter

explanation.surface: A choir rearranged so that the tenor's last note takes over from the bass, and the sound settles.
explanation.walkthrough: Both singers are letters rather than voices: a word for hopefulness has one letter swapped and becomes a phrase for stillness. 'Hopefully' is the raw material of the wordplay, not a comment on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something at rest has stopped moving and stopped fretting, which is what calling it calm says about it.

clue.text: Originally, baker oversupplied lightly — 13 — he often leaves éclair in safe place

indicators.note: originally means taking the starting letter of each following word

parts.note: the number 13, written out as thirteen, begins with T
the first letter of éclair, its accent dropped

explanation.surface: A baker who has overstocked lets a customer slip away with an éclair.
explanation.walkthrough: The 13 looks like a reference to another clue, but here it is just the number thirteen.
explanation.definitionFit: A bolthole is a hideaway where someone can escape and be safe.

clue.text: Zero tolerance finally adopted during time off

indicators.note: What comes finally in a word is its last letter, and that is all the clue takes from it.
Something adopted during an event is taken in while it is going on, so the letter lands inside the longer word.

parts.note: time off work is a rest
the last letter of TOLERANCE

explanation.surface: A zero-tolerance policy that finally gets taken up over the holidays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zero tolerance' is one phrase on the surface and splits down the middle underneath: the first word defines and the second is only a letter store.
explanation.definitionFit: To zero an instrument is to send it back to nought, which is the same instruction as resetting it.

clue.text: Slightly rotten greeting yelled

indicators.note: A greeting yelled across a street reaches you as noise, so it is the sound of the word on offer and not its spelling.

parts.note: the greeting is 'hi', and the answer is said in exactly that way

explanation.surface: A shouted hello that has gone a bit off.
explanation.walkthrough: Game birds are hung until they are high — just beginning to turn, and deliberately so, because that is when the flavour arrives. Two letters of sound buy four of spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat or game left hanging until it is on the turn is said to be high: rotten, but only slightly and on purpose.

clue.text: Intrude, all agitated and surly

indicators.note: An agitated liquid has everything in it churned out of place, so the letters will not stay where they were put.

parts.note: ten letters, exactly what the answer needs

explanation.surface: Barging in, thoroughly worked up and bad-tempered with it.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'Intrude' makes it read as an order, which hides the fact that it is only a supply of letters. Someone ill-natured is sour by disposition rather than sour today.
explanation.definitionFit: An ill-natured person is bad-tempered by nature, which is what calling them surly says of them.

clue.text: The reverse of 'dark' and 'night'?

indicators.note: The reverse of a word is both that word written backwards and that word's opposite, and one sense is used on each of the two quoted words.

parts.note: the opposite of night
dark is DIM, set down backwards

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks are the fairest signal in the puzzle: they mark two words to be operated on, not two words to be read for sense. Read straight, the whole clue is a true statement about the hour it names.
explanation.definitionFit: Midday is when the sun stands highest, the point of the day furthest from darkness and from night, so the clue read straight describes it.

clue.text: Was Spice Girl impersonating duck that's low-pitched and resonant?

definitions.note: The answer is an instrument and the definition an adjective phrase: the setter describes the noise the thing makes, and the question mark owns the liberty.

parts.note: DID stands in for WAS the way 'how do you do' stands in for 'how are you'
Geri Halliwell, Ginger Spice of the 1990s group
to do somebody is to do an impression of them
a batsman out without scoring makes a duck, written as a nought on the scorecard

explanation.surface: One of the Spice Girls doing a duck impression and booming away while she does it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' is the pivot: it looks like the bird being imitated and is a cricketing nought. The instrument is the Aboriginal Australian wooden drone pipe.
explanation.definitionFit: A didgeridoo is a long wooden drone pipe from Aboriginal Australia, and the single sustained buzzing note it makes is about as low-pitched and resonant as instruments get.

clue.text: And also not included in song: Hamilton's lead wanting direction

indicators.note: What is included in something sits inside it, so the short word goes within the longer one.

parts.note: a duet is a song for two voices
'nor' is exactly the word that means 'and also not'

indicators.note: A lead goes in front, so the letter wanted is the one at the head of the word.

parts.note: the leading letter of the title

explanation.surface: The star of Hamilton left out of a number and crying out for someone to direct him.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes 'song: Hamilton' read as one title, so two separate jobs look joined. Hamilton is the Lin-Manuel Miranda musical, and only its first letter is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Due north is north exactly, with no easterly or westerly lean, so the phrase names a compass direction.

clue.text: Middle of Feb, day in early May, or one late in Dec?

definitions.note: The definition works by example: the answer is not December's alone, but the two everybody can name fall in its last week.

indicators.note: The middle of a three-letter word is its second letter, the one with a letter either side of it.

parts.note: the middle letter of the three-letter month
VE Day, 8 May, marks victory in Europe in 1945 and is still commemorated in Britain

explanation.surface: Three dates picked off the calendar: one in February, one in May, one just before the new year.
explanation.walkthrough: Two of the three month names are only letter-stores and the third is the definition. Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve are the December ones the clue points at.
explanation.definitionFit: An eve is the day or evening before a feast, and Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve both fall in December's last week.

clue.text: Gunman's order delivered with difficulty, it's implied

definitions.note: The second half is not a dictionary sense: something won hands down is won easily, so the setter offers the hands the other way up as implying the opposite, and 'it's implied' admits as much.
definitions.meaning: the two words a robber shouts while pointing the gun
a thing done hands down is done easily, so turning the hands the other way round is meant to turn the sense round too

explanation.surface: A stick-up where the robber can barely get the words out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hands down' is the phrase the second half leans on: it means with ease, and inverting the hands is meant to invert the sense. The clue flags the invention with 'it's implied' rather than claiming it as usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Hands up is what a gunman shouts to make a victim raise their arms; and because hands down means easily, the same hands raised are offered as its opposite.

clue.text: Sunhats: oddly ignored means of preserving life

indicators.note: Ignoring a word's odd letters leaves the ones standing in the even positions, read off in order.

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of SUNHATS

explanation.surface: Sunhats written off, when wearing one is a way of keeping yourself alive.
explanation.walkthrough: UHT is ultra heat treatment, the scalding that produces the long-life milk on British supermarket shelves. 'Oddly' is doing arithmetic here, not describing how the hats were dismissed.
explanation.definitionFit: UHT gives milk a shelf life of months without a fridge, so the process is a means of preserving something's life — long life, as the carton says.

clue.text: Excellent: room's confining, at last, Bruno Mars

indicators.note: To confine somebody is to shut them in, so the letters doing the confining close round what comes next.

parts.note: def is slang for excellent, a dictionary word since hip-hop took it up
rms is the estate agent's short form for rooms

indicators.note: Taking a name at last takes it at its final letter and goes no further back into it.

parts.note: the last letter of BRUNO

explanation.surface: A cramped venue that has finally got Bruno Mars onto its stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bruno Mars' has to be split down the middle: the forename gives up a letter and the surname is a verb meaning to spoil. That verb is the entire definition, which is why the clue looks as though it has none.
explanation.definitionFit: To deform something is to spoil its shape, and 'mars' is the plain verb for spoiling — same tense, same job.

clue.text: Composition part #2

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a self-contained section of a symphony, concerto or sonata
second meaning: 'number two' is the nursery euphemism for defecation

explanation.surface: A terse catalogue label for the second section of some piece of music.
explanation.walkthrough: '#2' reads as numbering the composition's second section, but on its own it is 'number two', the childish euphemism for a bowel movement.
explanation.definitionFit: A symphony is divided into sections, each with its own tempo, and 'number two' is slang for defecation, also called a bowel evacuation.

clue.text: Sicilians possibly expelling a Milanese, awkwardly

indicators.note: To expel something is to throw it out, and what gets thrown out here is the letter A.
Letters handled awkwardly come out in the wrong order, which is the licence to rearrange them.

parts.note: the eight letters of MILANESE with the A expelled

explanation.surface: Sicilians running a man from Milan out of town.
explanation.walkthrough: The north-south quarrel does all the misdirection: 'Milanese' is not a nationality here but a bag of letters. 'Possibly' is fair warning that the answer covers islanders in general.
explanation.definitionFit: Isle men are men of an island, and Sicilians are one island's worth of them — which is the liberty 'possibly' concedes.

clue.text: Zoned out: this is ignoring the writer's parts

indicators.note: Something out is out of true, so the letters it describes are no longer to be trusted in the order given.
A word ignoring a letter leaves it out, so what follows is struck from what went before.

parts.note: the five letters of ZONED rebuilt
THIS without its I
a setter writing about himself is I, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: A reader gone blank, skipping straight past the bits the author wrote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zoned out' is one idiom on the surface and two separate jobs underneath. A dozenth is a twelfth, which is why the plural can mean parts at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A dozenth is a twelfth — one part of something split twelve ways — so the plural names fractional parts.

clue.text: Character in Globe — Roneo? — Not quite

indicators.note: What is in a run of words is literally inside it, already spelt out by letters sitting there in order.
Not quite all of what is offered is wanted, so the answer stops short of both ends of it.

parts.note: the run straddles the two words: glOBE RONeo

explanation.surface: Somebody at the Globe guessing at a character's name and being told they are close.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that Roneo is not quite Romeo — a Roneo was the office duplicating machine British schools once ran worksheets off. Oberon is the fairy king of A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: Oberon is a character in A Midsummer Night's Dream, the Shakespeare the Globe on Bankside exists to stage.

clue.text: Figure set around mostly satisfactory constant

indicators.note: around means the set wraps around the next piece

parts.note: a TV is a television set

indicators.note: mostly means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: well can mean satisfactory, as in 'all is well'
e is the mathematical constant, about 2.718

explanation.surface: A number arranged around a fairly good fixed value.
explanation.definitionFit: Twelve is a number, which can be called a figure.

clue.text: Former student crowned by those people — wise guys

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer a collective singular: 'wise guys' names the members, and the answer names the outfit they belong to.

indicators.note: A crown sits on top, so in a down entry whatever crowns the rest is written above it.

parts.note: 'them' is the pronoun for those people
OB is an old boy, the standard short form for a school's former pupil

explanation.surface: An old boy of the school being crowned by a crowd of self-styled clever types.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wise guys' is American for made men of the Mafia, not for clever-clogs, which is the sense the surface pushes. 'Crowned by' only works because this is a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Wise guy' is what members of the American Mafia call one another, and the Mob is the Mafia.

clue.text: Border has shown up throttling power in world? Not half

definitions.note: The definition is a joke rather than a synonym: the answer is half a world, and 'not half' is the setter conceding that it falls short of a whole one.

parts.note: a hem is the border stitched round a piece of cloth

indicators.note: To throttle something is to get both hands round its throat, so the letters doing the throttling close around what follows.

parts.note: somebody who has shown up is here
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: A frontier that has appeared out of nowhere and is strangling the world's power supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has shown up' reads as one verb and is two separate words underneath, which is where the clue hides. 'Not half' is British for 'very much indeed', the opposite of the sense wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A hemisphere is one half of the globe, so it is a world but, as the setter admits, not a whole one.

clue.text: Peep Show regularly lost money in Philippines

indicators.note: The letters lost are the ones at regular intervals — every second one — and what survives is read off in order.

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of PEEPSHOW

explanation.surface: A television comedy that kept on losing money out in the Philippines.
explanation.walkthrough: Peep Show is the Channel 4 sitcom shot from its characters' own eyeline, and the clue wants every other letter of its title. The peso is Philippine as well as Latin American.
explanation.definitionFit: The peso has been the currency of the Philippines since Spanish rule, so it is the money you spend there.

clue.text: Relief: American sizes successively decreasing

indicators.note: Each size named is smaller than the one before, so they are written down in that falling order.

parts.note: A is the standard short form for American
the letters on a clothing label: large, medium, small

explanation.surface: A relief shipment of American clothing, the sizes getting smaller down the pile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relief' looks like the heading on an aid bulletin and is the definition outright. Alms is the old word for money or food given to the poor, and it is always plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Alms are the money or food handed out to the poor, which is relief in its charitable sense rather than its easing-of-pain sense.

clue.text: Miles — perhaps not 500 — in cars offered here

definitions.note: The definition describes a place rather than giving a synonym: the answer is a firm's name, and the clue says what happens at its counter.

indicators.note: 'Not' strikes out what it names, so the numeral that follows is taken out of the letters.

parts.note: Miles Davis the jazz trumpeter is one Miles among several, which is what 'perhaps' concedes
D is 500 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A mileage, probably not five hundred of them, covered in a car hired for the week.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miles' has to become a surname before the clue works, and 500 has to become a Roman numeral. Avis is the hire company whose 'We try harder' slogan ran for decades.
explanation.definitionFit: Avis is one of the big car-hire chains, so its counter is exactly where cars are offered.

clue.text: I'm surprised by cellists' kit that's heard in woodwinds

indicators.note: that's heard says the combination is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: O, an exclamation of surprise, beside bows, the kit cellists play with, said together as O-BOWS

explanation.surface: Someone is startled that string players' gear can be heard among the wind instruments.
explanation.walkthrough: O plus BOWS, said aloud, sounds like the name of the reed instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: Oboes are double-reed instruments in the woodwind section of an orchestra.

clue.text: Rebutted curt prig with one book, The Agony and the Ecstasy?

definitions.note: The title is offered as an example rather than a synonym: agony and ecstasy are two of these, and the question mark owns it.

indicators.note: To rebut is to push back, so everything it governs is written out backwards.
A curt reply is cut short, so the word it describes loses its last letter.

parts.note: a prig is a SNOB, cut short to SNO and then turned round
one is I and a book a TOME; I TOME written backwards

explanation.surface: Answering back to a sniffy bore by handing him a single novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversal governs the whole of the wordplay, which is why its pieces arrive back to front. The Agony and the Ecstasy is Irving Stone's novel about Michelangelo, filmed in 1965.
explanation.definitionFit: Agony and ecstasy are feelings at the two extremes, so the title names a pair of emotions — examples, as the question mark admits.
